cross_source_notes: Meaning of khandha: both say 'heap/group' (P L36–L42; M L10). Only the Pradeepika lists the other senses of the word (quality, designation, convention) and explicitly sets them aside.

Materiality: the Margaya counts rūpa as the 28 material phenomena (M L10). The Pradeepika uses other frames: 25 rūpa-portions, 96 rūpas counted by kalāpa (P L61–L63), and 'all matter from the four origins' (P L79). These are different counting schemes and should not be merged into one number.

Feeling and perception: both identify these as single mental factors (P L81–L83; M L12–L14). The Pradeepika also classifies them six-fold by contact door and eleven-fold by aspect; lines 1–36 of the Margaya have neither.

Formations: both give 50 mental factors (P L85; M L16). The Pradeepika presents the heap through its chief member, intention, six-fold by contact (P L540–L557). The Margaya instead warns about the two meanings of 'saṅkhāra' (M L22).

Consciousness: both give 89 cittas (P L87; M L18). The Pradeepika lists it as seven at L77 (five sense-consciousnesses plus mind-element and mind-consciousness-element) and as six at L675–L682. Both are standard ways of dividing it, not a conflict.
Exclusion of nibbāna: both agree (P L990; M L20). Only the Margaya gives the reason: nibbāna has no past/future division, so there is no 'heap' of it.

Purpose of the five-way division: both tie it to loosening self-view. The Pradeepika presents this as the Buddha's teaching intention and the 'exactly five' argument (P L984, L996–L1010). The Margaya gives everyday first-person examples for each aggregate (M L24).

Aggregates of clinging: the Margaya defines upādāna as the two, craving and view, and limits the clinging aggregates to the worldly ones (81 worldly cittas), whose purpose is to mark out what to contemplate in insight (M L28–L34). The Pradeepika (in this part) describes them as objects of the four āsavas and four upādānas (P L992–L994). Its own definition of the four upādānas falls just after this part's range (L1206 onward).

Scope asymmetry: the eleven-aspect analysis, the sixteen-fold analysis, the ordering and 'exactly five' arguments, and all the similes (hospital, prison, meal, foam, bubble, mirage, plantain, conjuring) appear only in the Pradeepika. The Margaya's lesson 8 is a short textbook summary.

Clinging: P names four kinds of clinging [C077-P:L1208]. M defines clinging only as craving plus wrong view, 'mine' and 'I' [C077-M:L28]. Both agree that only worldly states are aggregates of clinging, with 81 worldly minds and 50 remaining mental factors [C077-P:L1216–L1222; C077-M:L30–L34].

Purpose: M says the five aggregates of clinging are taught to mark off what is to be taken up for insight [C077-M:L28]. P says they belong to the 'ground of insight' [C077-P:L1218]. These agree in substance.

Order of the twelve bases: P's table and discourse order pairs each door with its object (eye–form, ear–sound …) [C077-P:L1230–L1237]. P explains that the Abhidhamma order lists internal then external, unmixed [C077-P:L1403–L1407]. M gives only the internal-then-external list [C077-M:L41] and names the two groups [C077-M:L45].

Meaning of 'base': P gives several etymologies (striving, spreading, leading to long suffering; dwelling, support, meeting place, birthplace, cause) [C077-P:L1271–L1293]. M gives one functional definition: the place where mind and mental factors arise and perform their tasks, organised by the six doors [C077-M:L47].

Why three sortings: M states that the bases serve those who take mental activity as self, and the elements serve those who take consciousness as self [C077-M:L49; C077-M:L60]. P states the elements' purpose in the same terms [C077-P:L1853]. In this range P has no explicit statement that the bases target a particular self-view. P instead teaches the bases as empty and ownerless [C077-P:L1333–L1399].

Mind-object base or element: both give 52 mental factors + 16 subtle matter + the unconditioned [C077-M:L43; C077-M:L58; C077-P:L1409]. P counts this as 69 items at L1409 but as 20 at L1865, where the three mental aggregates are counted as three units. This is a difference in counting convention, not in content.

Mind-base: M says it is all 89 minds [C077-M:L43]. P's 'detailed' account gives it 81 varieties and explicitly excludes the 8 supramundane minds [C077-P:L1323], but a few lines later P calls the mind-base and object-base four-planed, mixing worldly and supramundane [C077-P:L1417]. The sources are best kept side by side here.

Order of the eighteen elements: P's table groups them in triads (door, object, consciousness), with mind-element 16, object-element 17 and mind-consciousness element 18 [C077-P:L1431–L1439]. M lists the five doors, five objects, five consciousnesses, then mind-element, mind-consciousness element and object-element [C077-M:L54]. The membership is identical.

Coverage: only P has the discourse-style three sextets, the long earth, water, fire, air, space and consciousness sections with body-part similes, the 35 other elements folded into the 18, and the closing similes [C077-P:L1421–L1895]. M's range has no element-by-element material and is a short classroom summary.

Scope: the Pradeepika gives a long treatment of about 1,130 lines (meanings, word-meaning, characteristics, why four, teaching order, similes, the four-way analysis, emptiness, each kind of suffering, craving, cessation, and the path before and at the path moment). The Margaya's Lesson 10 is a 45-line summary (M L63–L107).

Membership of the dukkha truth: the Pradeepika describes it as all three-plane dhammas except craving and the taint-free (P L2174). The Margaya counts it as 81 mundane cittas, 51 cetasikas other than lobha, and 28 rūpas (M L77, L103). The substance is compatible, but one describes and the other counts. Keep both.

Samudaya: the Margaya equates it with craving, identified as the lobha cetasika, and explains it as delight in the five aggregates as good and pleasant, which drives kamma (M L91, L103). The Pradeepika gives the threefold craving, ponobbhavikā, nandirāga and the sixty places (P L2780–L2830). In its four-way analysis it also calls other defilements, and even mundane wholesome states, 'samudaya but not the noble truth' (P L2250), a point the Margaya does not make.

The three kinds of suffering are defined differently. The Pradeepika: vipariṇāma-dukkha = pleasant feeling that becomes suffering when it changes; saṅkhāra-dukkha = neutral feeling and other three-plane formations oppressed by arising and passing (P L2440–L2442). The Margaya: saṅkhāra-dukkha = the toil of producing and maintaining a human existence (making merit, avoiding wrong, feeding, protecting); vipariṇāma-dukkha = the decay and breaking-up of formations (M L83–L85). Do not merge these.

Lists of kinds of suffering: the Pradeepika gives seven types (P L2428–L2452), a twelve-term list it attributes to Abhidhamma teaching (P L2454–L2467), and an eight-term list with vyādhi (sickness) that it attributes to the suttas (P L2469–L2473). The Margaya gives an eight-item list that folds sorrow and lamentation together and has no separate pain, grief, sickness or five-aggregates item (M L79). It then adds the three kinds (M L81–L87).

Nirodha: the Pradeepika defines it as the remainderless fading and cessation of craving, unconditioned and not mixed with any formation (P L2180, L2834). The Margaya explains it as the cessation of the five aggregates (M L95), with the note that 'five aggregates' here means mundane dhammas only (M L99).

Magga: the Margaya restricts the path truth to the eight factors in the supramundane path consciousness (M L99, L103). The Pradeepika discusses the factors both before the path (mundane, with different objects and different minds) and at the path moment, and says the Buddha taught the path truth as mundane and supramundane (P L2911, L3001, L3013).

Dhammas outside the truths: the Margaya lists the supramundane wholesome cittas, cetasikas other than the eight path factors, and the four fruition cittas with their cetasikas as outside the truths (M L105). The Pradeepika's four-way analysis agrees (P L2256, L2273, L2288), but at P L2231 it also calls path-associated states and fruition states 'dukkha' in the sense of saṅkhāra-dukkha, though not the noble truth of dukkha.

Meaning of 'ariya': the two sources agree. The Margaya adds 'supreme truth' and the point that some truths are true in one way and false in another (M L69); the Pradeepika adds tatha/avitatha/anaññatha and 'the Tathāgata's truths' (P L2050–L2058).

Chapter naming: the Pradeepika's closing refers to 'සව් සංග්‍රහය' and explains why khandha, āyatana, dhātu and sacca teachings exist, namely for beings confused about nāma, rūpa or both (P L3023–L3031). The Margaya's closing line names the chapter 'සමුච්චය සංග්‍රහ' (M L107) and has no equivalent explanation. The merge should reconcile this naming with the concept title සර්ව සංග්‍රහය.
uncertainties: P L61: the list of the 25 rūpa-portions is garbled. 'උපරිය සන්තති' is probably an OCR error for 'උපචය සන්තති', and the two alternative ways of reaching 15 subtle rūpas (excluding the heart-base, or merging upacaya+santati and including it) run together. Needs checking against the printed page (pdf 344).

P L432 and L450: 'පටිස සම්ඵස්සජා' is presumably paṭigha-samphassa (sense-impingement contact), which the text itself equates with five-door perception. But L432 glosses it as 'ක්‍රොධය හා ස්පශීයෙන්' (contact with anger), which does not fit that meaning. This may be an authorial gloss or an OCR/transcription slip; expert check needed.

P L828 vs L954: the list names the 16th mode as 'සබ්භාව', but the exposition discusses 'සඞ්ඛත/අසඞ්ඛත'. Also, modes 13–14 (paccaya, samuṭṭhāna) are only referred back to the 'රූප කාණ්ඩය' (L950), which is not in this extract. Not filled in.

P L878–L890: the editor's comment notes that the listed cittas that do not produce rūpa in the formless realm add up to 38, not the printed 'දෙසාළිස්' (42). The shortfall is probably the four arūpāvacara kiriyā cittas. Transcribed as printed; not corrected.

P L452: 'බාල බුහුණනිය' (the woman the young monk says he looked at 'as' a younger kinswoman) is unclear. The kin term may be misprinted. The anecdote's point (five-door perception can be read from how someone looks) is clear.
P L984: 'සත බහල භාවය' is probably an OCR error for 'ඝන බහල' (compactness), which is what the argument requires. Flagged, not corrected in citations.

P L219: the near/far ladder says another being 'even lying in one's own belly' is far, then that the child in one's belly is near. This reads as a relative, stepwise scale. A literal reading looks contradictory; expert confirmation of the intended sense is advisable before using it on screen.

P L960: the statement that attainment of cessation and name-concepts 'are called nipphanna' because they are entered or taken up by a person is compressed and possibly corrupted; doctrinal check needed.
Systematic OCR pattern throughout P: the repha is rendered as 'ී' or dropped (ස්පශීය = ස්පර්ශය, සථිති = ස්ථිති, චතුරාය්‍ය = චතුරාර්ය). Citations use the text as printed.

P L838 (size of the kalala), L1044 ('eighty families of worms') and the hell and ghost narratives at L103–L119 are traditional commentary material, not empirical claims. They should not be used on screen as facts about embryology or biology.
P L1016: perception is likened to the 'three humours' (තුන් දොස) as the proximate cause of illness. The stated reason is compressed; worth an expert check if the hospital simile is used.

Boundary: this part stops at P L1205. The Pradeepika's formal section on the aggregates of clinging (පඤ්චුපාදානස්කන්ධ, from L1206) belongs to Part 2 and is not summarised here, apart from the khandha/upādānakkhandha distinction that appears at P L988–L994.

C077-P L1210 says all states of both the round (vaṭṭa) and its cessation (vivaṭṭa) are included in the 'aggregate count', and L1214 identifies vivaṭṭa as the nibbāna-element. This appears to conflict with the standard position, stated in M L20 (outside this part's range), that nibbāna is not an aggregate. The sentence may refer to the whole compendium rather than the aggregates. It needs an expert check, and I have not resolved it.

C077-P L1393 says the not-self mark is hidden 'by continuity (santati)', the same cause given for impermanence at L1389. The commentarial tradition usually says not-self is hidden by 'compactness' (ghana). This could be a source error, an OCR error or a deliberate reading, and it needs checking against the printed page (pdf 438 / printed 427).
C077-P L1867 writes 'සැත්තෑ (76)': the word means seventy but the numeral says 76. M L58 says 76 ('සැත්තෑසය'). The word has probably been truncated, but this is not verified.

C077-P L1323 (mind-base = 81, supramundane excluded), P L1417 (mind-base four-planed) and M L43 (mind-base = 89) give different scopes. This is probably context-dependent (the insight context versus the full classification), but it needs an expert check.

C077-P L1327 runs together the sentence on sound-base varieties ('ශබ්දායතනයෙහි ප්‍රභෙද දෙකෙකි') and the like/unlike (sabhāga/visabhāga) classification without naming the two kinds of sound. Text may be missing.

Recurring OCR pattern in P: 'වාර' for 'ද්වාර' (door) and 'වාදසායතන' for 'ද්වාදසායතන' (twelve bases) (e.g. L1271–L1303, L1403, L1417), and 'විධ' with the 'ද්වි' prefix missing (L1467, L1477, L1609). Likely OCR errors with probable readings: 'බුරසා' L1691 (probably ඛුරකා, razor-winds), 'බුරවක්‍රය' L1889 (probably ඛුරචක්‍රය, razor-wheel), 'ෂඩි' L1385 (probably ඍද්ධි), 'ඉගුළු' L1397, 'ඡෙය්‍ය' L1461, 'ද්‍රේද' L1597, 'සාතු' L1697 and 'උක්තල' L1873. These readings are my guesses and have not been adopted as fact.

Organ names in the earth-element list (C077-P L1475, L1545–L1557: 'දලබු', 'බඩදිව', 'පපුමස', 'අතුණු බහන') need an expert check before they are given English anatomical equivalents. I have not translated them in this digest.

The metal classification at C077-P L1583–L1585 ('පිසාච ලොහ' and its eight named kinds) is obscure, and the names may be corrupted. It is not used in the explanation beyond the general list of outer earth.
C077-M L28 has a garbled phrase ('උපාදානයන්ට හසුවන නො වන ධර්ම දෙ කොටස ම'), which probably means 'both the grasped and the non-grasped'. I read it that way, but it is a typo in the source.

The plain five aggregates (M L4–L24, and the corresponding P material before L1206) and the four truths (P from L1901; also anticipated at P L1745) fall outside this part's range. Part 1 and Part 3 should reconcile them.

The Pradeepika text has systematic font-conversion artefacts: 'ී' stands for 'ර්' (අථී = අර්ථ, මාගී = මාර්ග, දගීන = දර්ශන, ගභී = ගර්භ, වීයයී = වීර්ය); 'ඩ' stands for 'ද්ධ' (බුඩ, සිඩ, ශ්‍රඩා); 'ෙව' stands for ද්වේ/වෛ (ෙවෂ, ෙවර); and 'විධ' appears where 'ද්විවිධ' is meant (e.g. L2324, L2336, L2350, L2364, L2558, L2567, L2640). The Sinhala explanation normalises these readings; an expert should confirm them.

L1972 and L1976 'හෙඩාථීය' is read as hetu-attha (හේතු/හේත්වර්ථ); this is inferred. The same samudaya meaning is spelled 'පලිබොධාථීය' at L1948 but 'පරිරොධාර්ථය' at L2000, and L1976 has 'පරිරොධ ධම්'. These are probably palibodha/paribodha misprints; not resolved.
The printed folio '446' at L2026 is a misprint for 476, as noted by the transcriber (L2028–L2032).
The numbering of right view's three functions is misprinted at L2895–L2899 (1, 1, 2), per the transcriber's note L2901–L2905.

In the four-way analysis of dukkha, item 3 (L2235) and item 4 (L2237–L2241) are internally confusing. A parenthetical about 'the truth one enters the dispensation to understand' is not a noble truth 'by its knowable nature', and item 3 calls samudaya and magga 'dukkha' through impermanence. Text may be missing or corrupted. It has not been interpreted here and needs expert reading.
In the three-friends simile the tree is 'සපු' (champak) at L2384 but 'සල්' (sal) at L2386. This is an internal inconsistency.

The attribution of the twelve-term list to 'Abhidhamma teaching' and of the eight-term list with vyādhi to the suttas (L2454–L2473) is the Pradeepika's claim. It has not been checked against canonical texts and needs expert verification.

'දුක්ඛ දුක්ඛය' is used in two senses. At L2438 it means painful feeling, bodily and mental. In the twelve-term list (L2461) and under the heading at L2694–L2696 it covers bodily pain only, with domanassa listed separately.
At L2300–L2304 the path truth is said to be empty of permanence, pleasure and self, but 'subha' is not listed, whereas the first two truths are empty of all four. This may be intended or an omission.
L2965 'කණු කැමැති බව' is probably 'කනු කැමැති' (wanting to eat), a typo reading.
L2754 'ඉතා මැතව' is probably 'ඉතා මැනවි' (L2756 has 'මැනවී'). This is a typo reading.
In the Margaya, lines 63–107 contain no page markers, so the printed page cannot be cited for this range.
The Margaya closes the chapter as 'සමුච්චය සංග්‍රහ' [C077-M:L107], while the concept is titled 'සර්ව සංග්‍රහය' (the section heading within that chapter); both names are kept.

Pradeepika's text has systematic font-conversion errors (e.g. 'ී' for 'ර්', so 'මාගී' = 'මාර්ග'). Quotations in the Sinhala explanation were normalised by the reader and need an expert check against the scan.
